newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: RED CROSS: last hope for broken lives.
newsitem.headline: RED CROSS: last hope for broken lives.

text.p: The International Committee of the Red Cross, which lost six workers in a terror attack in Chechnya on Tuesday, is a last hope for the damned and the dying in the world's most dangerous war zones.

The Swiss-run ICRC looks after the sick, traces lost children, visits prisoners, helps mine victims, feeds the hungry and saves lives in the frontline of emergencies from east Zaire, Rwanda and Somalia to ex-Yugoslavia, Tajikistan and Afghanistan.
Its humanitarian work depends on its neutrality and fragile trust. It does not take sides in political, racial, religious or ideological conflicts and cherishes its independence.

Increasingly, the ICRC's work involves more than coping with emergencies but longer term help such as in Rwanda where it helped to build new prisons to ease the suffering of 90,000 Hutu suspects of the 1994 genocide in overcrowded jails.
The ICRC, with more than 8,000 workers, takes a leading part in enforcing international law governing the use of weapons in war, treatment of prisoners and civilians.
A Red Cross leaflet for fighters in war zones reads: "Fight only combatants, attack only military targets, spare civilian objects, restrict destruction to what your mission requires."
But such rules are rarely obeyed in dangerous and isolated war zones, where the lives of ICRC workers are often at risk.
ICRC official Kim Gordon Bates said 1996 was the worst year.
"The number of security incidents against our staff members runs into pages. But 1996 was the worst -- we had three people killed in Burundi and now six in Chechnya," he told Reuters.
In Burundi, ravaged by a vicious three-year war between the mainly Tutsi army and majority Hutu rebels, three Swiss ICRC employees were murdered in an ambush on a mountain road in June.
In Somalia earlier this year, six local Red Cross volunteers were injured when trying to evacuate wounded.
Recently in east Zaire, a Red Cross plane trying to locate refugees lost in the tropical forests was hit by a stray bullet.

The ICRC last made the headlines a week ago, when its three staff members were freed from 38 days of rebel captivity in southern Sudan by U.S. congressman Bill Richardson, named Washington's new ambassador to the United Nations on Friday.
The Australian nurse, American pilot and a Kenyan colleague were freed after Richardson bargained rebels' demand for a $100 million ransom down to five tonnes of rice, jeeps and radios.
The ICRC's image was tarnished and neutrality challenged when U.S. intelligence documents declassified this year claimed it was penetrated by Nazi agents during the second world war.
One document, dated 1946, referred to ICRC employees who used their position to carry enemy funds and enemy-owned jewels across the Swiss frontier. The ICRC rejected the claims.

The Red Cross concept of humanitarian service was founded in 1863 by a young Geneva businessman, Henry Dunant, after he witnessed the battlefield horrors of Solferino in 1859 and organised a relief operation with local help.
This became the founding organisation of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement.
ICRC's work is based on the 1949 Geneva Conventions on treatment of civilians during conflict, signed by 135 countries, and 164 national Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies.
One witness to the agency's grim history is the Red Cross museum in Geneva.

It has the world's longest telegramme -- 72 metres long -- sent by Washington to the agency in 1943 and containing the names of all German soldiers captured by allied soldiers and transferred to the United States.
